description: Zaragoza students in engineering, physics and maths, going for the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. Carlos and Roberto (Mechanical Engineering + Finance) work on orbital mechanics and space debris. We will build an intuitive tool to compare lunar south pole landing sites: Sun and Earth over the horizon, power and comms windows. We look for: web visualization, DEMs, SPICE.
summary: We set out to build a tool that lets mission planners, educators and the general public compare landing sites and dates near the lunar South Pole. For any site and date, the tool should answer two practical questions: what is the illumination (power generation), and is the Earth above the local horizon (direct-to-Earth communication). Because the South Pole has very low Sun and Earth elevations and especially steep terrain, small changes in position or date can change the answer completely. Our approach combines three ingredients: Sun and Earth ephemerides expressed in a Moon-fixed frame, real NASA LOLA elevation maps of the South Pole, and computational-geometry algorithms that decide whether the line of sight from the site to the Sun or the Earth is blocked by the terrain.
details:
Data collection: terrain height, orientation and coordinates of the Moon (spherical coordinates), plus the positions of the Sun and the Earth over time. We used data from the LOLA elevation models for the topography of the south pole, NASA GMAT to simulate 11 years of Sun and Earth positions overtime.

Discretising the Moon (mesh): a coarse mesh far from the landing site and a fine mesh close to it, built from parallels and meridians while avoiding degenerate polar caps, together with the maximum horizon distance that has to be meshed. The main loop buids, for every moment in time, the segment from the point of interest and the celestial body of interest and checks if it intersects with the mesh. That way, we can see if there is direct line of sight with the body and the angle of illumination in case of the sun.

Displaying in web application: We built a web interface for planning missions to the South Pole (84°S–90°S). Users choose a site from a catalogue of real locations or enter their own coordinates, pick a date range and mission filters (mast height, communication band, antenna diameter, direct-to-Earth or relay link), and get:

● Sun elevation, illumination percentage and irradiance;

● Direct-to-Earth and relay communication coverage;

● Estimated slope and temperature;

● An overall site score from 0 to 10, the best landing windows, and a side-by-side comparison of two sites or two dates.

The physics engine is written in C++17 and runs behind a small local HTTP server. A mirror engine in JavaScript lets the same site run as a static page on GitHub Pages, so anyone can open it from a link.

The mesh approach allows the code to take into consideration the angle of incidence of sunlight, making the calculation of the relative illuminance possible. The system to define this mesh is made from scratch, and it allows for the point of interest to be in the center of a face in the patch, which will make the measuring process of the angle of illumination more accurate, making the prediction better. It is also a fairly optimized algorithm, which is an advantage with respect to other algorithms for defining the mesh. The algorithm was made to create a patch of triangles that are equilateral if we don’t take into account the altitude of each point in the moon, and though it was mostly written with AI, it was written with this purpose.

We opted to make the algorithms somewhat loyal to classic physics approaches to these kinds of problems for many reasons, including the expandability of the code to other problems and the adaptability of the application to process different data (we simulated 11 years with GMAT, but the code could read and process any other dataset with minimal change). Overall, the code is versatile and functions more as an engine and general solution for the problem rather than a specific one, and could be used to solve similar problems concerning other celestial bodies, or even in whole other fields, without modifying almost anything from the code.
